headline: High: Pipecat’s shared-bus, multi-API defaults can cascade untrusted content and sensitive data into broad network egress; the other profile is a non-runnable content list with limited direct interaction.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no runnable I/O surfaces beyond broad network egress and is a content-writing list, so direct injection into A is not evidenced. B uses a shared bus across instances and ingests text/audio/video, so if A’s outputs are manually bridged into B, prompt-like content could influence B. The pathway is indirect and not default between these profiles.
conditions: IF A’s content is copied into B’s shared bus or text input
IF B treats inbound text from A as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable any manual copy-paste bridge between A and B
Add a provenance tag to all A-originated text before B ingests it
Configure B to reject instruction-like content from untrusted sources
Use a separate bus or namespace for A-originated messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: B touches text, conversation state, audio, video, images, and has allowlisted network egress, so sensitive material can leave the local boundary in default integrations. A is a content-writing profile with broad network egress but no data classes touched, so it is not the main leakage source. The pair creates a plausible leakage path through B’s external API calls.
conditions: IF B is configured with any external STT/LLM/TTS/analytics provider
IF sensitive text, audio, images, or conversation state are routed through B
mitigations: Restrict B to local-only providers where possible
Remove analytics/telemetry endpoints from B configuration
Redact sensitive fields before B sends requests
Separate sensitive workloads from B’s shared bus
Audit outbound destinations in B’s allowlist

C_capability_conflict.rationale: B explicitly supports multiple instances with shared bus state, which creates write contention risk on shared mutable resources. A exposes broad network egress, so if it participates in the same workflow it can also emit conflicting updates or side effects. No locking or isolation is documented for the pair, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF A and B write to the same downstream resource or bus
IF B instances run concurrently without external locking
mitigations: Assign separate namespaces or queues per instance
Add an external lock around shared writes
Serialize writes from A and B to the same resource
Disable multi-instance sharing for B where feasible

D_cascading_error.rationale: B can consume text and conversation state from its shared bus, so A-originated content could be treated as upstream input if bridged. A is a content-writing profile, making it plausible that B renders or acts on A’s generated text without verification. The pair lacks documented validation steps, so the cascade risk is real but not shown to trigger irreversible actions by default.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated text from the shared bus
IF B forwards A’s output to downstream actions without verification
mitigations: Insert a verification step before B acts on A output
Require human review for A-generated instructions
Mark A output as advisory only in B prompts
Log and diff A output before downstream use

E_compliance.rationale: No specific residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for A or B, and neither profile lists regulated data classes like PHI. B’s analytics/metrics and external service integrations create some compliance surface, while A’s broad egress is generic. Because the pairwise compliance pathway is undocumented, this remains a low, gap-based concern.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through B’s external providers
IF retention or residency requirements apply to the deployed environment
mitigations: Disable telemetry and analytics in B
Keep regulated data out of B’s external calls
Document provider residency for each B integration
Review retention settings before deployment
